challenges.name: Grounds Streak
challenges.note: Eight correct actions in a row

hazards.bypass-backflow-assembly: You opened the bypass valve around the backflow assembly. That bypass exists for emergencies with its own procedure, and opening it during a routine test connects the irrigation side straight to the drinking water supply with nothing left to stop fertiliser, pesticide residue or standing lawn water from siphoning back into it.
hazards.hot-panel-no-lockout: You opened the controller panel before the breaker was locked out. A panel that looks like a low-voltage timer on the outside still has a line-voltage feed behind that cover, and opening it on a guess instead of a locked-out and verified breaker is how a routine schedule change turns into a shock.
hazards.reach-into-flooded-box: You reached bare-handed into a flooded valve box with a wiring splice sitting in the water. Standing water around an energised splice does not announce which puddle is live and which is not, and a gloved hand reaching in blind is trusting a guess a multimeter or a walk-around would have settled first.
hazards.test-cock-under-pressure: You opened a test cock before the assembly was properly isolated. A test cock opened on a line that is still fully pressurised does not trickle — it sprays hard enough to reach an unprotected face, which is exactly the moment eye protection and a slow, deliberate valve sequence both exist for.

interrupts.alert: A second zone valve has stuck open and its sprinkler heads are still spraying even though this zone's own shutoff is holding.
interrupts.cue: Close the second zone's manual shutoff before the drain-down continues.
interrupts.missNote: The second zone kept spraying while the drain-down continued. A system that is not actually isolated is not actually safe to open downstream of.
interrupts.why: A drain-down that assumes one shutoff speaks for the whole system misses exactly this — a second zone with its own stuck valve keeps pressurising the line the crew believes is draining, and closing that second shutoff by hand is the only way to actually get the system to the state the work plan assumes it is already in.
interrupts.wrongNote: Not that — close the second zone's manual shutoff before anything else about this drain-down matters.

interrupts.alert: The flow reading has spiked and a lateral line has broken underground, sending a geyser up through the turf ahead.
interrupts.cue: Close the emergency shutoff before the break erodes any more of the bed.
interrupts.missNote: The geyser kept running while the flow reading stayed high. A break like this gets worse, not better, the longer the line stays pressurised.
interrupts.why: A broken lateral line under pressure does not slow down while someone walks back to read the manual — the flow reading spiking is the system's own warning, and the emergency shutoff is what actually stops the geyser before it undermines the turf around it or floods a bed nobody meant to water at all.
interrupts.wrongNote: Not that — the emergency shutoff is what this break needs, before anything else about this walk continues.

lateNotes.hose-to-cock1: The test procedure's own hose order exists because each connection references the pressure the one before it just set — out of order, the reading on the gauge does not mean what the procedure needs it to mean.
lateNotes.stuck-valve: A valve that will not turn by hand is a valve that gets worked with the proper tool and a plan, not forced — force on a stuck valve is how a body snaps instead of a stem turning free.

name: Irrigation Controller, Valve Box & Backflow Check

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check the current watering schedule against the water agency's own days before changing anything.
steps.prompt: Check the current watering schedule against the water agency's own days before changing anything.
steps.title: Read the controller's current schedule
steps.why: A schedule changed without first reading what is actually programmed risks undoing a setting the last service call made for a reason nobody wrote down — reading the current programme first is what keeps today's fix from becoming tomorrow's mystery.

steps.cue: Eye protection and work gloves before the panel or the valve box are opened.
steps.prompt: Eye protection and work gloves before the panel or the valve box are opened.
steps.title: Suit up before opening anything
steps.why: A backflow test cock opened under pressure and a valve box with wiring and standing water both reward the same two pieces of PPE — eye protection against a spray nobody planned for, and gloves against a splice or a sharp fitting a bare hand would otherwise find first.

steps.cue: Lock out the circuit breaker feeding the controller before opening its panel.
steps.prompt: Lock out the circuit breaker feeding the controller before opening its panel.
steps.title: Lock out the controller's breaker
steps.why: A controller enclosure that looks like a low-voltage timer on the outside still carries a line-voltage feed behind the cover, and locking the breaker out before opening it is what turns a guess about whether it is de-energised into a fact the technician does not have to trust blind.

steps.cue: Three things about this valve box are not what they look like from a standing start — find them before a hand goes near it.

decoyNotes.intact-valve-box: That valve box is dry, its lid is seated and nothing inside looks disturbed. Nothing to flag there.

itemNames.stuck-valve: the valve that will not turn free
itemNames.wiring-splice: the wiring splice sitting in standing water

itemNotes.cracked-lid: A cracked lid is a tripping hazard on the turf and an open invitation for whatever is living under it before anyone's hand goes near the box.
itemNotes.stuck-valve: A valve that resists turning is telling the technician something before it ever gets forced — force on a seized valve is how a stem snaps instead of a valve opening.
itemNotes.wiring-splice: A splice sitting in standing water is exactly the kind of thing a bare hand should never find out about by feel.

steps.prompt: Three things about this valve box are not what they look like from a standing start — find them before a hand goes near it.
steps.title: Walk the valve box before reaching in
steps.why: A valve box that looks routine from above is not the same thing as a valve box someone has actually looked into, and a cracked lid, a seized valve or a submerged splice are exactly what a walk-around catches before a gloved hand finds them the hard way.

steps.cue: Pry the lid with the tool, check for standing water, and inspect the wiring before reaching inside.
steps.prompt: Pry the lid with the tool, check for standing water, and inspect the wiring before reaching inside.
steps.title: Open the valve box properly
steps.why: Prying the lid with a tool instead of fingers, checking for standing water and inspecting the wiring before reaching in are the three habits that turn opening a valve box from a blind reach into a checked, deliberate step.

steps.cue: Turn the zone's own shutoff valve closed before disconnecting anything downstream.
steps.prompt: Turn the zone's own shutoff valve closed before disconnecting anything downstream.
steps.title: Isolate the zone before working on it
steps.why: Isolating the zone at its own shutoff before disconnecting fittings downstream is what keeps a routine repair from becoming a pressurised line spraying the technician the moment a fitting comes apart.

steps.cue: Carry the test kit from the truck to the backflow assembly before connecting anything.

drag.missNote: Not at the assembly — carry the test kit to where the backflow assembly actually is.

steps.prompt: Carry the test kit from the truck to the backflow assembly before connecting anything.
steps.title: Stage the backflow test kit
steps.why: Staging the whole test kit at the assembly before the first hose goes on means the test procedure runs start to finish without a walk back to the truck partway through with a test cock already open.

steps.cue: Connect the hose to test cock one, then test cock two, then bleed the air from both lines.

itemNames.bleed-air: bleed the air from the hoses

steps.outOfOrderNote: That is out of the test procedure's own order. Cock one, then cock two, then bleed the air — out of order, the differential reading does not mean what the procedure needs it to mean.
steps.prompt: Connect the hose to test cock one, then test cock two, then bleed the air from both lines.
steps.title: Connect the test hoses in the procedure's order
steps.why: The test procedure's hose order exists because each connection sets up the reference pressure the next one is measured against — connecting them out of order, or skipping the air bleed, gives a differential reading that looks like a result but is not actually measuring what the procedure needs it to measure.

steps.cue: Read the gauge and commit only inside the band the test procedure calls a pass.

gauge.label: DIFFERENTIAL PRESSURE
gauge.missNote: Outside the passing band per the test procedure. Bleed the lines again and let the reading settle before committing it.

steps.prompt: Read the gauge and commit only inside the band the test procedure calls a pass.
steps.title: Read the differential pressure
steps.why: The differential pressure reading is the actual proof the check valve inside the assembly is holding — committing it only inside the procedure's own passing band is what makes this a test rather than a glance at a needle that looked about right.

steps.cue: Check the backflow assembly's own tag for the last certified test date before logging a new one.
steps.prompt: Check the backflow assembly's own tag for the last certified test date before logging a new one.
steps.title: Confirm the tester's certification tag
steps.why: The assembly's certification tag is what the water agency and the next inspection both check — confirming the last date before adding a new one is what keeps the record honest about when this device was actually last proven to hold.

steps.cue: Hold the shutoff valve closed for the full drain-down before disconnecting the test hoses.
steps.holdBreakNote: Let go of the shutoff before the line finished draining. Hold it closed for the full drain-down, every time.
steps.prompt: Hold the shutoff valve closed for the full drain-down before disconnecting the test hoses.
steps.title: Hold the shutoff closed while the line drains
steps.why: A shutoff released early lets the line re-pressurise while the test hoses are still connected, which is exactly how a fitting under pressure comes apart in someone's hands instead of on a bench with the system actually drained.

steps.cue: Keep the flow reading steady in band while walking the zone to confirm every head fires correctly.
steps.holdBreakNote: The flow reading drifted out of band during the walk. Bring the zone back to a steady reading before calling the walk finished.
steps.prompt: Keep the flow reading steady in band while walking the zone to confirm every head fires correctly.
steps.title: Walk the zone under the flow meter's reading
steps.why: A steady flow reading while walking the zone is what confirms every head is firing the way the system expects — a reading that drifts out of band partway through the walk is the system's own way of saying a head is clogged, broken or missing before anyone has to find that out by eye alone.

steps.cue: Set the run times to the season and the water agency's own days, never a plain reset.
steps.prompt: Set the run times to the season and the water agency's own days, never a plain reset.
steps.title: Set the controller's programme
steps.why: Resetting the controller to its factory default undoes every adjustment a past service call made for this specific site's sun, soil and slope — setting the programme to the season and the water agency's own days is what keeps today's fix from being tomorrow's overwatered bed.

steps.cue: Log the valve box findings, the test result and the programme change before leaving the site.
steps.prompt: Log the valve box findings, the test result and the programme change before leaving the site.
steps.title: Close out the service call log
steps.why: The service log is what the next technician and the next inspection both read — a call handled cleanly but never logged leaves nothing behind to prove the valve box was checked, the assembly tested, and the programme actually set on purpose.
